name: Kripapureeswarar Temple, Thiruvennainallur
deity: Shiva as Kripapureeswarar (Thaduthatkonda Nathar), with the Goddess Mangalambigai
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, where Sundarar sang his first hymn (8th century); Chola temple of the 10th century
summary: Here, by the Pennai, the Lord stopped Sundarar's wedding with a palm-leaf deed, claimed him as his own, and drew from him his first hymn — 'Pittha pirai soodi', the opening of the seventh Tirumurai.

sections.history: Thiruvennainallur is a small town of Viluppuram district on the southern bank of the Pennai, about 19 km from Villupuram on the road between Panruti and Thirukkovilur. Its temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Tevaram and one of the most beloved in Nadu Nadu, for this is where Sundarar's life as a saint began and where he sang his first pathigam, 'Pittha pirai soodi', which opens the seventh Tirumurai. The present stone temple is Chola work, believed to date from the tenth century and perhaps renewed in the time of Uttama Chola; the queen Sembiyan Mahadevi is remembered among its patrons, and its inscriptions speak of temple gardens. The town is also honoured as the home of Meykandar, whose Sivagnana Bodham became the foundation text of Shaiva Siddhanta.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex of the Chola period, its shrines enclosed by a granite wall and entered beneath a tiered rajagopuram. Within, the Lord is worshipped as a lingam in a sanctum approached through the ardha mandapa and mukha mandapa, the pillared halls before the shrine. The Goddess Mangalambigai has her own shrine, and the temple's Vinayaka is honoured as the one who, tradition says, initiated the child Meykandar.
sections.legends: On the day of Sundarar's wedding at Puthur, an aged Brahmin appeared with a palm-leaf deed declaring that Sundarar and his line were his bondsmen. Sundarar called him a madman — pittha — and the dispute was brought before the elders of Thiruvennainallur, who found the deed true. The old man led them to the temple and vanished into the sanctum: he was Shiva himself. The Lord bade Sundarar sing, beginning with the very word he had flung at him, and so the hymn opens 'Pittha'. From this the Lord is called Thaduthatkonda Nathar, the one who stopped him and made him his own.
sections.festivals: Sundarar's day in the month of Aadi (July–August) is kept with special devotion here, and Panguni Uthiram in March–April, with its float festival, is the temple's most prominent celebration. Maha Shivaratri and Karthigai Deepam follow the Shaiva calendar; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Pilgrims come to Thiruvennainallur to stand where the saint was claimed, and many recite 'Pittha pirai soodi' before the sanctum into which the old man vanished. Students of Shaiva Siddhanta come too, for Meykandar's sake. The Pennai-bank temples of Thiruvidaiyaru and Thirukkovilur lie close by and are easily joined to the visit.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvennainallur lies about 19 km from Villupuram on the Panruti–Thirukkovilur road, and is served by buses from Villupuram, Panruti and Thirukkovilur. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Chennai and Tiruchirappalli are the nearest major airports, with Puducherry also within reach by road.
